Return `429` with `Retry-After`. If you run more than one instance, the bucket state needs to live in a shared store (Redis) rather than in-process, otherwise limits are per-instance and easy to blow past by hitting different nodes.

The fork that actually matters: whether you enforce this at the gateway (nginx/Envoy/API gateway) or in app middleware. Gateway is faster to deploy, keeps limiting logic out of app code, and stops abusive traffic before it costs you compute — that's the one I'd pick unless you don't control the gateway layer. App-level middleware is easier if you need per-endpoint or per-plan-tier limits with business logic.

Left out: burst allowance tuning, per-endpoint vs global limits, and how to communicate limits to legitimate high-volume clients (higher tier, batch endpoints) — those are policy decisions once the mechanism's in place.

Extend `govern()`'s return to include an `alerts` list alongside `cap`/`state`/`guardrail`, computed from counters folded into the persisted state (SPEC already implies one such counter — the 3-cycle `feed_stale` streak; add matching streaks for cap-pinned-at-edge and pace-error-above-15%). The supervisor then just loops over `result.alerts` and calls `alert()` for each, the same way it already does for `quota_exceeded` at SPEC.md:31-32 — no new side-effecting logic in the loop, and the streak logic stays inside the pure core so it rides the existing unit-test and simulation-replay ladder.

One condition doesn't fit that shape: **heartbeat missed** (SPEC.md:66) can't come from `govern()`, since `govern()` only runs when the loop runs. That needs an external watchdog — something that checks each tenant's last-persisted-cycle timestamp against a threshold (5 min + slack) and fires independently of the control loop.

Left unspecified in SPEC.md: how `alert()` itself dedupes/delivers (paging vs. Slack vs. log-and-scrape) — that's a separate piece from the detection logic above.

The 0% CDN hit rate is the root cause, not a coincidence: `middleware/security.js` slaps `no-store` on every route app-wide, including `/p`, because the 2024 audit fix for the `/account` leak was applied globally to hit a deadline. The CDN (`CDN.md`) already sits in front and already respects whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends — it just has nothing to work with.

**Fix:** scope that middleware to `/account` only, and give `/p/:slug` its own `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=N` (it's anonymous, no session read, same for everyone — safe to cache at the edge). That alone removes the DB from the hot path for repeat requests, since `relatedProducts` (~600ms join) and `stockFor` (~250ms) are exactly the calls a cache hit skips.

Two decisions actually fork this design:

1. **Does `stockFor` belong inside the cached response?** Catalog data changes "a few times a day," but stock changes on every order — baking it into a page cached for, say, 5 minutes risks showing available stock that's gone. Either accept that staleness window (pick `s-maxage` to match what's tolerable, e.g. 30-60s with `stale-while-revalidate`), or drop `stockFor` out of `db.productBySlug`'s render and fetch it as a separate, uncached call so the cached shell is instant and stock stays live. The CDN has no ESI/fragment support ("no path rules"), so that split means a real second request, not an edge trick.
2. **Does anything ever make this page user-specific?** Right now `/p` reads no session, so it's safe to cache publicly at a shared edge key. If personalization (pricing, recommendations) gets added later, this whole approach breaks and you'd need per-user caching (Vary on a cookie, or move to client-side fetch) instead of a flat public cache.

Left out: an application-level cache (Redis) for `relatedProducts` in `db.js`. That's only worth adding if edge coverage stays incomplete after the header fix — start with the free win of not hitting origin at all.

Recommend: identify the client by API key (not IP — one client behind a proxy or NAT shouldn't cost others), enforce a per-key token bucket at the edge (API gateway/reverse proxy like Envoy/nginx, or middleware in front of the app) backed by Redis so limits hold across instances, and return `429` with a `Retry-After` header when exceeded.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Enforcement point**: gateway/edge vs. in-app middleware. Edge is better here since the goal is protecting the shared service before the offending traffic even reaches app logic; in-app only helps once you're already paying the cost.
- **Algorithm**: token bucket (allows bursts, smooths average rate) vs. fixed/sliding window (simpler, but can let a client spike to 2x limit at window boundaries). Token bucket is the better fit for "one client hammering" since it caps sustained rate while still tolerating normal burstiness from everyone else.

Depth I'm leaving out: per-route vs. global limits, and whether to throttle (delay) instead of reject — worth a follow-up once the enforcement point and algorithm are settled.

Two forks make this design non-trivial:

**1. The masking problem.** Guardrails are priority-ordered and `govern()` returns only the single winning one, but Observability needs alerts on `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, etc. even when a higher-priority guardrail (e.g. `quota_exceeded`) is the one actually driving the cap that cycle. If alerting keys off `result.guardrail` alone, a masked condition never fires. Fix: have `govern()` return a separate `signals` set — every condition that evaluated true this cycle — distinct from the single `guardrail` that governs the cap. The supervisor loops over `signals` and calls `alert()` for each, instead of the current one-off `if result.guardrail == "quota_exceeded"` check.

**2. Threshold conditions aren't guardrails.** "Cap pinned for two consecutive cycles" and "pace error >15% for two consecutive cycles" need cross-cycle counters, but that's exactly what the persisted `state` is for — add `clamp_streak` / `pace_error_streak` fields, increment/reset them inside `govern()`, and emit a signal when they cross threshold. This keeps the counting inside the pure core, so the simulation harness still replays it deterministically.

Everything else in the Observability list (`quota_exceeded`, `feed_stale`×3, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`) falls out of that same `signals` set, and the supervisor's job stays exactly what it already is for I/O: `for s in result.signals: alert(s, tenant)`.

The one item that can't come from `govern()` at all is **heartbeat missed** — that's the loop's *absence*, so it needs an external watchdog (dead-man's-switch on a per-tenant last-run timestamp) rather than anything inside the control loop.

Left out: alert delivery mechanics (dedup/re-notify cadence for conditions that stay true for hours, e.g. `quota_exceeded` holding at zero all day) — depends on what alerting backend you're targeting. Which one is that?

Every write in this service already funnels through one function — `db.write()` in `db.js:13` — so that's the choke point to instrument, rather than adding logging to each route.

**Design:**
1. Add an insert-only `audit_log` table (`actor_id, table_name, row_id, action, old_values jsonb, new_values jsonb, occurred_at`), with the app's DB role denied `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on it so a compromised app can't rewrite its own history.
2. Insert into it from inside `write()`'s existing transaction (`db.js:16-19`), right alongside the real write — same `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`, so the audit row and the change either both land or both roll back.
3. Thread the actor through: `write()` currently only sees SQL text and params, not `req.user` (set in `auth.js:11`). Cheapest fix is an `AsyncLocalStorage` context set once in `sessionUser`, so `write()` can read the current actor without changing every call site's signature.

**The real fork:** app-level capture (what's above) only sees writes that go through `db.write()` — it's blind to anyone hitting Postgres directly (migrations, a psql session, a future service). If the compliance requirement is "every write to these tables, full stop," you want Postgres triggers with `OLD`/`NEW` instead, which also gives you before/after values for free instead of needing a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before each `UPDATE`/`DELETE` to capture "before." App-level is simpler and gets you actor identity cleanly; triggers are the belt-and-suspenders answer if bypassing the app is a real threat model here. Worth deciding which one compliance actually needs before building.

Don't build a new caching layer — fix the one already in place. The CDN sits in front of every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the app sends (CDN.md), but it's at 0% hit rate because `middleware/security.js:8` applies `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` to every route, including `/p`. That header was the fast fix for a real finding — an `/account` page leaking to another user through an intermediary cache — but it got applied app-wide rather than scoped to `/account`, and `/p` has been paying for it since.

Product pages qualify for caching: `routes/products.js:6-8` notes they're anonymous, identical for every user, and only change when catalog data is edited (a few times a day). That covers `productBySlug` (40ms) and `relatedProducts` (600ms, the four-table join, and the biggest cost) cleanly — cache the rendered page at the edge with something like `public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=60`, and a cache hit skips the DB entirely.

Two things this forks on:

1. **Split the middleware, don't touch its logic.** Keep `no-store` on `/account` (that's the audit fix, don't weaken it) and give `/p` its own cacheable header. This is a header change, not new infrastructure — the CDN contract already says cache policy is the app's decision via headers, and they declined path rules last quarter, so this is the sanctioned lever.

2. **Stock is the outlier.** `stockFor` (`sum(quantity)`, 250ms) changes on every order, faster than the catalog does. Baking it into a 5-minute-cached page risks showing stale availability. Either accept that staleness at a short TTL (fine if exact stock isn't safety-critical to show instantly), or pull it out of the cached HTML and serve it as a small separate uncached call — you still avoid the 40ms + 600ms majority of the 900ms on every hit, just not the 250ms.

Left out: cache invalidation on product edits (purge-on-publish from the admin tool vs. just letting TTL expire) and whether `relatedProducts` ever needs to be per-request fresh — worth checking with whoever owns the catalog admin flow.

Rate-limit by client identity (API key, not IP — IPs get shared behind NAT/CDNs and rotated), enforced at the gateway/edge before requests reach app servers, using a token bucket per key: steady rate plus a small burst allowance, so a single client gets capped without needing to reject every spike.

The one fork that matters: are your /v1 servers stateless behind a load balancer, or a single instance? If multiple instances, the bucket state has to live in something shared (Redis INCR+EXPIRE or a Lua-scripted token bucket) — otherwise each instance enforces the limit independently and the effective ceiling is (limit × instance count). If it's a single instance or you already have an API gateway (Envoy/Kong/nginx) in front, enforce there and skip building it in-app.

Return `429` with `Retry-After` and expose `X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset` so well-behaved clients back off instead of retrying into the wall.

What's actually in front of /v1 right now — a gateway, a load balancer, or just app servers? That decides whether this is a config change or new code.

Polling, not push. `PLATFORM.md` rules out both alternatives: WebSocket upgrades return 501 at the edge, and SSE needs a connection held open past the response, which can't happen — instances are frozen between invocations and there's no sticky routing to bring a client back to the same one anyway. That's exactly why a manual-click model was built in the first place.

It's also worth noting there's no real freshness to chase: `rollup.md` says the table is overwritten once a minute, on the minute, and nothing else writes it. Polling faster than that buys nothing. So the fix is just changing `public/dashboard.js` from "call `load()` on click/page-load" to "call it every 60s" against the existing `/api/metrics` endpoint, which is already cheap (30ms, `no-store`) and already returns `computed_at`.

The one real decision: whether to align the poll to the minute boundary (fetch at, say, `:02` past each minute) for the tightest possible freshness, versus a plain `setInterval(load, 60_000)` from page-load, which is simpler but can lag up to a minute behind a rewrite depending on load-time offset. A cheap add-on given `computed_at` is already in the response: skip re-rendering when it's unchanged from the last poll, so the UI doesn't flicker every tick when the job hasn't run yet.

Left out: anything server-side — `api/metrics.js` and the rollup job don't need to change, since this is purely a client polling-cadence change against the endpoint that already exists.

Two things in the current code force the design: `payments.js` throws on timeout with no idempotency key, and `PROVIDER.md` says a timeout means **unknown, not failed** — the charge may have gone through. Right now a naive "just retry" would risk double-charging on the cases that actually succeeded server-side.

**Core fix:** send an `Idempotency-Key` header on every `POST /v2/charges` call, generated once per order (e.g. derived from `order.id`, since the route already gates on `status = 'pending'` so there's only ever one live attempt per order) and reused on every retry for that order. With the key in place, retrying a timed-out request is safe — the vendor either authorizes once or returns the original result, never a second charge.

That done, two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Inline vs. deferred retry.** Each vendor call can already take up to 10s; 2–3 serial retries could hold the HTTP request open 20–30s, which is its own bad UX. Simplest: 1–2 quick retries with short backoff inline in `payments.charge`, still within the request. If you want more resilience than that, don't block the request — set the order to `processing`, return that to the client, and reconcile in the background (a job or queue worker that retries with the same key and updates the order when it resolves).
2. **What "still unknown" means after retries are exhausted.** It must not collapse back to `502 "payment failed"` — that's the actual bug (timeout treated as failure). Land it on a distinct state, e.g. `processing`/`needs_reconciliation`, and resolve it later (retry again, or a status lookup if the vendor exposes one by idempotency key) rather than showing the customer a false failure.

Left out: retry policy for genuine 4xx/5xx (non-timeout) responses, and whether the vendor exposes a way to look up a charge by idempotency key instead of always retrying blind.

Recommendation: Postgres full-text search, not a new search service. Add a `tsvector` column combining name (weighted higher) and description, index it with GIN, rank results with `ts_rank`, and layer `pg_trgm` on top for typo/prefix tolerance on short queries — no new infrastructure, and it's fast enough up to hundreds of thousands of products.

The one fork worth deciding now: stay on Postgres vs. stand up a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Typesense/Elasticsearch). Pick the dedicated engine only if you need faceted filtering, sub-50ms latency at high query volume, or relevance tuning beyond what `ts_rank` gives you — otherwise it's added ops cost for no real gain next quarter.

Left out: synonym handling and semantic/embedding search for queries that don't share literal words with the product text — worth revisiting once basic keyword search ships and you see what people actually type.

The two decisions that fork this:

1. **Presigned direct-to-storage upload vs. proxying through your API.** Have the client request a signed upload URL from your server, upload the photo bytes straight to object storage (S3/GCS/etc.), then notify your server to create the listing-photo record. Proxying binary uploads through your app server doubles bandwidth/memory for no benefit once you're past a toy scale.
2. **Client-side compression before upload.** Phone camera shots run 3-12MB (often HEIC). Resize to something like 1600px on the long edge and re-encode as JPEG on-device before upload — this is the difference between a 1-2s upload and a 10s+ one on cellular. Server should still validate/re-derive dimensions rather than trust the client blindly.

Everything else (thumbnail generation, EXIF/GPS stripping, ordering/primary-photo flag, retry on flaky mobile networks) is the next layer down and depends on your stack — what's the mobile client (native/React Native/PWA) and storage backend?

Poll, not push — this platform rules out the alternative. `PLATFORM.md` says WebSocket handshakes 501 at the edge, and even SSE (a held-open HTTP response) can't work here: functions die at 10s and instances freeze between invocations, so nothing can sit waiting to push a change.

The good news: `rollup` (`jobs/rollup.md`) only changes once a minute, so "real-time" push wouldn't buy anything over polling anyway — the freshness ceiling is 1 minute no matter the transport.

Build it as: change `dashboard.js`'s `load()` from load-once-plus-button to `setInterval(load, 20000)` or so (comfortably under the 1-minute rollup cadence, way under the 10s function budget — `/api/metrics` already responds in 30ms). Keep the button for an on-demand check. That's the whole change; no backend work needed since `api/metrics.js` is already cheap and stateless.

One real decision: fixed-interval poll (simplest) vs. `computed_at`-aware polling that skips re-render when the timestamp hasn't moved. Given the response is 4KB/30ms, that optimization isn't worth the complexity — plain interval polling is the right call.

Depth left out: if `rollup` ever gets expensive to compute per-request or the platform's DB connection limits become a concern under many polling dashboards, that's a caching/rate-limiting question for `api/metrics.js`, not the update mechanism.

The real bug isn't "no retry" — it's that `payments.js:8-13` never sends an `Idempotency-Key`, so blindly retrying today would risk a second authorization. `PROVIDER.md` says the vendor treats a timeout as **unknown, not failed**, and guarantees that two requests sharing an `Idempotency-Key` within 24h return the same charge instead of double-charging. Fix that first — retries become safe as a consequence.

**Design:**

1. Generate one idempotency key per order (e.g. the order id itself, since an order should only ever produce one successful charge) and persist it to the `orders` row *before* calling the provider — so it survives a crash mid-request and any later retry, even from a different process, reuses the same key instead of minting a new one.
2. Send that key as `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for that order, first call and retries alike.
3. In `routes/checkout.js:16-28`, only retry on the `provider timeout` error — a 4xx from the vendor is a definite decline and should still surface immediately. Retry the same request with the same key, bounded (e.g. 2 attempts) with a short backoff.

**The fork:** sync vs. async retry.
- *Sync*: retry inline in the route handler, same request. Simplest, no new infra — but each retry costs up to another 10s (the existing per-call timeout), so the client-facing request can now run 20-30s, which needs its own timeout raised to match.
- *Async*: on first timeout, write `status = 'processing'` (a third state alongside `pending`/`paid`) with the idempotency key, return that to the client, and have a background job keep retrying with the same key/backoff until it gets a definitive charge id or decline, then flip status. Client polls or gets notified. More moving parts, but doesn't block the request and also covers the crash case where the server dies after calling the provider but before writing `paid` — something sync retry doesn't fix.

Given this fires only a few times a day, I'd lean async and reuse the existing `status` column for the third state.

Left out: exact backoff/attempt tuning, and how the client is told once a `processing` order resolves (poll vs. webhook vs. email) — worth deciding once you pick sync vs. async.

Default to Postgres full-text search: add a `tsvector` column combining name (weighted `A`) and description (weighted `B`), index it with GIN, and rank results with `ts_rank`. That's fast to ship, needs no new infra, and handles "a few words" queries well.

The one fork worth deciding now: does the catalog need typo-tolerance/instant-as-you-type relevance (e.g., thousands+ SKUs, consumer-facing search-as-you-type)? If yes, skip Postgres and use Meilisearch or Algolia instead — better fuzzy matching and ranking out of the box, but adds an external service and a sync pipeline to keep it consistent with the DB. If the catalog is small/mid-sized and "good enough" relevance is fine, Postgres full-text search is the simpler call.

So proxying upload bytes through the app server isn't viable. Upload straight to S3 with a signed PUT URL instead — storage.js:14-16 already generates these (the PUT branch is unused), and the bucket's CORS already permits PUT from market.example.com (storage.js:12), so no infra changes are needed.

Flow: client asks the API for a signed PUT URL (e.g. `POST /:id/photos/sign` calling `storage.signedUrl(key, {method:'PUT'})`), uploads the file directly to S3 from the phone/browser, then confirms back (e.g. `POST /:id/photos` with the key) so the server appends it via `db.addPhotoKey` (db.js:10-12) — the reverse of the existing invoice read path (routes/listings.js:14-17).

- Whether the confirm step trusts the client's claim that the PUT succeeded, or verifies with a `HeadObjectCommand` before writing the key — trusting it means `photo_keys` can end up referencing objects that were never uploaded.
- Whether that confirm endpoint checks who's allowed to write to the listing — nothing in routes/listings.js currently checks ownership on any route.

Two decisions actually fork this:

**Transport.** If the dashboard only needs to receive updates (no client-to-server data), use Server-Sent Events — plain HTTP, auto-reconnect built in, simpler than WebSockets. Reach for WebSockets only if you already need bidirectional traffic (e.g., users can act on the dashboard and expect other viewers to see it). Plain short-interval polling is the fallback if your infra can't hold long-lived connections (serverless functions, certain load balancers).

**What triggers a push.** Either the backend recomputes on a timer and pushes if the result changed (simple, but adds latency up to the timer period and wasted work when nothing changed), or it reacts to the underlying data change itself — a DB trigger/CDC stream/pub-sub event on whatever writes the metrics — and pushes immediately. Event-driven is the better fit for "ops dashboard," since staleness during an incident is exactly what you're trying to kill.

Recommendation: SSE endpoint fed by whatever event/queue system already emits on the underlying data changes; client keeps one connection open and patches the DOM/state on each message.

Left out: auth on long-lived connections, reconnect/backoff behavior, and fan-out if this scales past a handful of concurrent viewers (pub-sub broker vs. one process holding all connections).

Read the actual code: `payments.js` makes one call to Cardstream with no retry, `PROVIDER.md` states the vendor's own rule — a timeout means **unknown**, not failed, and idempotency keys exist but aren't used — and `routes/checkout.js` catches everything, including timeouts, and reports "payment failed."

That last point is why blind retrying would be dangerous here: on a timeout you don't know if the issuer already authorized the charge, so retrying without reusing the same request means a real risk of double-charging a customer who then sees two charges instead of one failure.

**The fix has two parts:**

1. **Idempotency key per order, reused on every attempt.** Generate it once (e.g. `order-${order.id}` or a UUID) when the order first enters checkout, store it on the order row, and send it as `Idempotency-Key` on the first request and every retry. Cardstream then guarantees a retry after a timeout returns the original charge rather than authorizing again — this is what actually makes retrying safe, not the retry loop itself.

2. **Classify the failure before deciding to retry.** In `payments.js`, a timeout or connection error is retryable (the vendor is telling you the outcome is unknown); a 4xx from the provider (declined, insufficient funds) is a real answer and must not be retried — retrying a decline just wastes an attempt and delays the correct "payment failed" message.

**Where the retry loop goes:** this route is synchronous request/response with no job queue anywhere in the stack, so the natural fit is a bounded retry loop inside `payments.charge()` itself — a few attempts with short backoff (rate limit is 600/min, nowhere close to a concern) — rather than introducing async processing. The route handler in `checkout.js` doesn't need to change its shape; it just ends up only seeing a rejection once retries are exhausted, so "payment failed" becomes true again instead of meaning "we gave up after one timeout."

At 38k rows growing by a few hundred a month, Postgres full-text search on the existing `products` table beats standing up Elasticsearch/Algolia — one less service, and the volume doesn't need it.

Add a generated `tsvector` column weighted toward `name` over `description`, index it with GIN, and query with `websearch_to_tsquery` plus `ts_rank` for ordering:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vec tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;
CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vec);
```

Then a `GET /products?q=...` in `routes/products.js`, same paging shape as the existing list route, filtering `WHERE active AND search_vec @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)` ordered by `ts_rank`.

The one real fork: plain `tsvector` matching is exact-word (stems, not typos) — "wireles" won't match "wireless". A timeout means "unknown state," not "failed" — the charge may have actually gone through on the processor's side. Retrying blindly on that assumption is what risks double-charging; the fix is idempotency plus reconciliation, not just a retry loop.

Design:
1. **Idempotency key per attempt.** Generate one (e.g. `order_id:attempt_id`) and pass it on every charge request. Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a second charge (Stripe/Braintree/Adyen all support this natively).
2. **On timeout, reconcile before deciding anything.** Enqueue a worker job that queries the processor for that key's status: succeeded → mark the order paid; declined → genuine failure; still pending/unknown → retry the same request with backoff, capped at N attempts.
3. **Split "declined" from "timeout" as separate states.** Only a real decline from the processor should produce the generic "payment failed" message. A timeout should route to "processing" (or a silent retry) — that's the actual bug behind what the customer sees today.
4. **Put this server-side**, in a queue/worker, not the client. The client that experienced the timeout has no way to know if the charge landed, so it shouldn't be the one deciding to resubmit.

- Whether the processor supports idempotency keys natively — if not, you need your own stored reference plus a "did this charge happen" lookup before any retry.
- Sync vs async UX: does the customer wait through the reconcile+retry cycle, or see "processing" and get a webhook/email update later.

Left out: specific backoff/attempt-count values, and webhook vs polling for the status check — both depend on your processor's API and how long you're willing to keep the customer waiting.

Add a `tsvector` generated column over `name || description`, index it with GIN, and query with `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles multi-word input the way users actually type it) ranked by `ts_rank`. New route: `GET /products/search?q=...`, parallel to the existing paged listing.

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vec tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;
CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vec);
```

The two decisions that actually fork this: generated-column-plus-GIN (fast, stays in sync automatically, costs one migration) versus computing `to_tsvector` inline per query (no migration, but no index, so it's a seq scan every search — fine at 38K rows today, but that's the thing to revisit if the table ever grows past a few hundred K). And `websearch_to_tsquery` over `plainto_tsquery`, since it tolerates the quotes/OR/minus syntax users paste in without erroring like `to_tsquery` does on raw input.

Query shape, weighting `name` matches above `description` matches:

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents
FROM products
WHERE active AND search_vec @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)
ORDER BY ts_rank(search_vec, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)) DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

Recommendation: mint an idempotency key once per order, persist it before the first charge attempt (e.g. a `charge_key` column on `orders`, set in the same transaction that reads the row), send it as `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for that order, and retry only on timeout/connection error — not on a 4xx, which is a real decline — with a small bounded attempt count and backoff. Because the key is stable and stored server-side rather than regenerated per call, a retry after a timeout replays safely: Cardstream returns the original charge if it already went through, or authorizes fresh if it didn't.

Left out: exact backoff/attempt-count values, and schema for the reconciliation job if you go out-of-band — those are the next-level-down details once you pick a side on the two forks above.

At that point you still don't know the outcome, so `checkout.js` can't honestly return "paid" or "failed" — the honest response is something like "processing" (202), with reconciliation happening out of band later (a poll against the vendor keyed on the idempotency key, or a webhook if Cardstream sends one). The core problem: a timeout doesn't tell you whether the charge actually went through server-side — so a naive retry risks a double charge, and "payment failed" is often just a lie. Fix that first, then the retry loop is easy.

**Design:**

1. **Idempotency key per charge attempt.** Generate one key for the logical purchase and reuse it on every retry. Stripe/Braintree/Adyen etc. all dedupe on this — a retried request with the same key returns the original result instead of charging twice. If you're not already passing one, this is the prerequisite, not an optional hardening step.
2. **On timeout, reconcile before retrying.** Query the processor for that idempotency key's actual status first. It may have succeeded despite the client-side timeout. Only retry if the query also fails or comes back "no such charge."
3. **Retry only ambiguous/transient failures** — timeouts, network errors, 5xx — with backoff and a small cap (e.g. 3 attempts). Hard declines (insufficient funds, card declined) are terminal; retrying those just annoys the customer.
4. **Own the state, don't trust the request/response cycle.** Track each attempt (pending/succeeded/failed) in your DB keyed by the idempotency key. That's what drives the retry loop and what you show the customer — not the return value of one HTTP call.
5. **Stop showing "payment failed" for a timeout.** Show "processing," retry (steps 2–3) inline for a couple seconds, and if still unresolved fall back to an async job that finishes via webhook/polling. Only surface failure once retries and reconciliation are exhausted.

Which processor are you on — that determines the exact reconciliation call in step 2.

Given it's product search where users often mistype brand/model names, I'd lean toward including trigram from the start rather than bolting it on later.

Left out at this altitude: relevance tuning (weighting name vs description, boosting in-stock items), query parsing edge cases (multi-word phrases, stopwords), and pagination of ranked results — those are next-level-down decisions once the basic search route exists.

Direct-to-storage upload with client-side resize: the client downsizes/re-encodes the photo (cap ~2000px long edge, JPEG, bake EXIF orientation into pixels) then uploads straight to object storage via a short-lived presigned URL the server issues; the server just records a row (listing_id, storage key, order, status) once the client reports success, and generates thumbnails asynchronously off that key.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Direct-to-storage vs. proxying through your app server** — phone photos run several MB each, so routing them through your API doubles bandwidth/memory for no benefit. Presigned URLs let the client hit storage directly.
- **Client-side resize vs. uploading full-res and downsizing server-side** — mobile uplinks are slow and drop mid-upload, so shrinking first cuts time and wasted data; the fiddly part is decoding HEIC and fixing orientation client-side before re-encoding.

Left out: resumable/retry handling for dropped connections, thumbnail size variants and CDN serving, and any moderation/virus-scan step before a photo goes live.
